21707-ungava:
Fur traders push into the wild country around Hudson's Bay in this early novel by R. M. Ballantyne. In his introduction, Ballantyne says most of the main events really happened to the first settlers of Ungava. He reshaped real people and real dangers into a story, with their leader's own records as his base.

The tale opens in deep forest, with a rifle shot, hard counsel, and a narrow escape on an ice floe. Ballantyne had worked for the Hudson's Bay Company as a young man, so the cold, the travel, and the trade feel lived-in. It stands as one of the books that made his name with young readers.
21918-hindu-law-and-judicature-from-the-:
Ancient Hindu law reaches English readers in this 1859 translation of the law chapters of the Dharma-Shastra of Yajnavalkya. Edward Röer, a scholar of Sanskrit, worked with W. A. Montriou, a barrister, to join exact rendering with legal sense. The preface says a connected, explained translation was a practical want, and a long list of subscribers in India agreed. The great commentary, the Mitakshara, supplies the staple of their notes.

The rules cover courts, evidence, debts, inheritance, and the duties of kings in judgment. Yajnavalkya stands with Manu among the lawgivers of classical India. For British judges and Indian lawyers of 1859, this was a working tool. For readers now, it opens the legal mind of an old civilization in its own terms.

Altamura has 4 parishes and 19,333 Catholics; Acquaviva has one parish and 8,527 Catholics; the clergy number 80.

dutt-mahabharata-adi-parva:
Dutt's prose Mahabharata opens with the Adi Parva, Englished in 1895. The Book of Beginnings traces the Bharata line from its first kings. The princes' youth and the famed dice game fill its later span.

Feuds take root as Pandava and Kaurava cousins grow up rivals. Teachers, marriages, and exile shape the heroes of the coming war. Dutt aimed to give English readers the whole vast epic in prose. His was the first full English Mahabharata of its kind ever made. The world's longest epic starts its immense arc in this opening book. Every later grief grows from seeds planted in these early chapters.
dutt-mahabharata-anushasana-parva:
Anushasana Parva, the Book of Instruction, comes in Dutt's 1905 English. Bhishma's teachings from the arrow-bed reach their end in this volume. The old warrior answers the king's last questions on right conduct.

Duty, charity, gifts, and the rites owed to gods and kin fill the talks. Precept stands on precept in the epic's great didactic manner. Bhishma blesses the king, then yields his life at the chosen hour. The book completes the moral frame of the whole Mahabharata. Dutt's plain prose keeps the old counsel clear for modern readers today. The farewell to Bhishma lands with quiet, earned force at the end.
dutt-mahabharata-shanti-parva:
Shanti Parva, the Book of Peace, appears in Dutt's 1903 English version. After the great war, the dying Bhishma lies on a bed of arrows. From that bed he teaches the young king through long, calm talks.

Law, kingship, duty, and the good life unfold in his final lessons. He speaks to a world shattered by war and kin-killing. His counsel mixes hard statecraft with deep thought on fate and release. Many call this book the epic's deep core of wisdom. Rulers and plain readers alike have mined its teachings for ages. Its calm tone after so much slaughter gives the lessons extra weight.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile-cy:
For decades, governments in Latin America's Southern Cone trusted Crypto AG machines to keep their most secret messages safe. The CIA's Minerva Secret reveals who really stood behind the Swiss company: the CIA itself, as a hidden owner.

Operation Condor states used the firm's devices without knowing their supplier was American intelligence, which could read what the machines appeared to protect. The briefing book tells how the secret was kept for so long and what it yielded to Washington. It is a story about trust in technology, and about how one hidden ownership deal quietly opened the secret cables of half a continent.
nasa-tm-19660020065-development-of-ablat:
Peter J LeBel and James M Russell III at Langley developed sensors that ride inside a heat shield. The sensors report how fast the shield wears away in flight. Their paper was given in Los Angeles in October 1965. An ablative shield protects a reentry vehicle by melting and flowing off. Knowing how fast the surface recedes during flight is the key measure. Three sensor kinds are named: make wire, light pipe, and spring wire types.

Flight data from inside a working shield are hard to get any other way. Ground tests cannot copy a real entry in full. Sensors that survive long enough to report give designers the truth about their shield. Advanced reentry vehicles, named in the title, were the direct users of this work.
nasa-tm-19670007218-an-integrating-spher:
James B. Heaney, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in December 1966. It presents a coating that lets integrating spheres work in the vacuum ultraviolet. An integrating sphere collects reflected light evenly so total reflectance can be measured, but standard smoked magnesium oxide coatings fail at short wavelengths.

Heaney's solution uses the fluorescent properties of sodium salicylate. The sphere is first coated with a durable magnesium oxide paint that reflects well where sodium salicylate glows. A thin salicylate layer goes on top, sensitive to the short-wave radiation bounced off the sample. The pairing also reflects the resulting fluorescent light reasonably well. The paper describes the instrument used and reports tests on several matte samples.
nasa-tm-19670014580-dim-light-photograph:
L. Dunkelman and a co-author, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, prepared this briefing in February 1966. It covers photographing faint space phenomena, and watching them by eye, from crewed spacecraft. The preface says the document copies the written information given to the Gemini VI and VII crews before their flights.

NASA Headquarters had asked for these experiments on an opportunity basis. The first section treats the twilight scene, a continuing study of Schirra's bands and aerosol layers. Long-exposure color photography could catch the higher, fainter layers of air. The last pages reproduce the checklists carried aboard both spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19700026393-an-analysis-of-the-r:
B. H. Batson prepared this internal note at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston on November 1, 1968. It analyzes the relative merits of various PCM code formats. PCM, or pulse code modulation, is a way to send data as coded pulses from a spacecraft, turning measured levels into ones and zeros.

Batson notes that the range instrumentation group allowed seven digital formats for such streams. All seven, he explains, are variants of three basic shapes for writing a bit. They are non-return-to-zero, split-phase, and return-to-zero forms. One key difference among them is the transmission bandwidth each one demands. The analysis weighs the formats against each other so engineers could pick with the trade-offs in view.
twenty-four-short-sermons-on-the-doctrin:
John Bovee Dods, pastor of the First Universalist Society at Taunton, Massachusetts, printed Twenty-Four Short Sermons on the Doctrine of Universal Salvation at Boston in 1832. Sermon one takes its text from Psalm 34: keep the tongue from evil, depart from evil, and seek peace.

Dods begins with self-preservation, the desire to lengthen life that clings to people even in pain and misery. Regulating the passions, he argues, does more for health and long life than climate or diet. Malice, envy, and revenge corrode body and soul alike, while tenderness, compassion, and hope multiply a person's years. Universalist preaching here starts from daily conduct rather than doctrine.
